extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent practitioners referencing USPTO guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for performing the Step 2A (Alice/Mayo first-part) patent-eligibility analysis to determine whether a claim is "directed to" a judicial exception (abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon), including how to identify exceptions, when to proceed to Step 2B, and how to treat computer-related improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims whose BRI covers statutory and non-statutory embodiments
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim whose broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) covers both statutory and non-statutory embodiments embraces subject matter that is not eligible for patent protection and therefore is directed to non-statutory subject matter (Step 1: NO).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such claims fail Step 1 and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 101; best practice is for the examiner to point out the BRI and recommend an amendment, if possible, to narrow the claim to those embodiments that fall within a statutory category. Example: machine-readable media whose BRI encompasses transitory carrier waves should be rejected as non-statutory (see In re Nuijten; Mentor Graphics v. EVE-USA).

rubrics_metrics.name: If claim is not within statutory categories (Step 1: NO)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a claim is clearly not within one of the four enumerated categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter), then a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 must be made indicating the claim is directed to non-statutory subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.01 and see MPEP § 706.03(a). However, if the disclosure suggests the claim could be amended to fall within a statutory category, proceed to analyze whether such an amended claim would be eligible at Pathway A, B, or C, and recommend amendment if possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial exceptions and the preemption concern
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to abstract ideas (including mathematical algorithms), natural phenomena, and laws of nature are not eligible for patent protection; the Supreme Court's concern underlying these exceptions is preemption (monopolization of basic tools of scientific and technological work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preemption is the concern but not a standalone test; questions of preemption are inherent in and resolved by the Alice/Mayo two-part framework (Steps 2A and 2B). The absence of complete preemption does not demonstrate eligibility, and newly discovered concepts can still be judicial exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A: Determine whether a claim is directed to a judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 2A asks whether the claim is 'directed to' a law of nature, natural phenomenon (product of nature), or an abstract idea. A claim is directed to a judicial exception when a judicial exception is recited (set forth or described) in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recitation can occur in different ways (explicit discrete language or broader description). If the claim as a whole is not directed to an exception (Step 2A: NO), it is eligible at Pathway B. If directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES), proceed to Step 2B to determine whether the claim amounts to significantly more than the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish claims that 'recite' an exception from those that merely 'involve' one
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should distinguish claims that recite an exception (which require further eligibility analysis) from claims that merely involve an exception (which are eligible and do not require further eligibility analysis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the claim as a whole. Example: a claim explicitly reciting F=ma recites a law of nature (directed to an exception); a teeter-totter claim that does not recite the law of the lever merely involves the natural principle and is eligible without further analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid parsing a recited exception into multiple exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless it is clear that the claim recites distinct exceptions, care should be taken not to parse a recited exception into multiple exceptions, particularly for abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, a series of mental steps manipulating information should be treated as a single abstract idea rather than multiple separate abstract ideas. However, if a claim recites multiple exceptions, it is directed to at least one judicial exception and must be analyzed in Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to identify an abstract idea in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should determine whether a claim recites an abstract idea by (1) identifying the claimed concept (the specific claim limitation(s) the examiner believes may be an abstract idea), and (2) comparing that claimed concept to concepts previously identified by the courts as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claimed concept is similar to one or more court-identified abstract ideas, it is reasonable to conclude the concept is an abstract idea (Step 2A: YES) and proceed to Step 2B. If not similar and no basis exists to conclude it is an abstract idea, find the claim not directed to an abstract idea (Step 2A: NO), unless another exception is recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to improvements in computer functionality or other technology are not abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventions that pertain to improvements in computer functionality or other technologies are not abstract when appropriately claimed and may be eligible at Step 2A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit examples include Enfish (self-referential database), McRO (automatic lip synchronization using particular computer-implemented rules), and Visual Memory (enhanced computer memory system). When claiming an improvement, the specification should disclose sufficient details such that one of ordinary skill recognizes the claimed invention as providing an improvement, and the claim itself must reflect the improvement in technology. Examiners must give the claim its BRI and evaluate both claim and specification; consider whether the claim covers a particular solution or merely the idea of a solution, and whether the BRI is limited to computer implementation. See MPEP § 2106.05(a) for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: What does not show an improvement to computer-functionality or technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain features do not demonstrate an improvement in computer functionality or other technology even if computer-related: e.g., processes that can be performed without a computer, mere automation of manual processes, speed increases that stem solely from general-purpose computer capabilities, or conventional implementation on generic components.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit guidance: if a claimed process can be performed mentally or without a computer (Synopsys v. Mentor Graphics), it cannot be characterized as an improvement in a computer. Mere automation or implementation on generic components/machinery (Affinity Labs; TLI Communications; FairWarning; Credit Acceptance) is insufficient. Examiners should consider these cases and MPEP § 2106.05(a) for further examples and discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve computer/technology improvement question early where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Although whether a claim improves computer-functionality or other technology may be considered in either Step 2A or Step 2B, examiners are encouraged to resolve this question as early as possible in the eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear improvement (e.g., Enfish) could be found eligible at Pathway A under the streamlined analysis or at Pathway B as not being directed to an abstract idea. If the improvement is not clear enough for Step 2A, it may nonetheless contribute to eligibility in Step 2B. Use the streamlined procedures in MPEP § 2106.06(b) as appropriate.
